aiOverview.content: Cancer is a group of over 100 diseases characterized by uncontrolled cell growth that can invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body (metastasis). Caused by genetic mutations from environmental factors, lifestyle, or inheritance, it is diagnosed via scans, labs, and biopsies. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and newer targeted therapies. How Cancer is Diagnosed Imaging Tests: CT scans, MRIs, X-rays, and PET scans help identify tumor locations and sizes. Biopsy: A tissue sample is removed and examined under a microscope, which is often the definitive way to diagnose cancer. Laboratory Tests: Blood and urine tests can detect abnormal cell counts or specific tumor markers. Physical Exam/History: Initial detection based on symptoms and checking for abnormal lumps. Treatment Options Surgery: Aims to remove the tumor, often effective for localized cancers. Chemotherapy: Uses drugs to kill rapidly dividing cancer cells throughout the body. Radiation Therapy: Uses high-energy radiation to target and kill cancer cells. Targeted Therapy & Immunotherapy: Newer treatments that target specific genetic changes in cancer cells or boost the immune system to fight the cancer. Key Aspects & Latest Advancements Metastasis: The biggest threat is when cancer spreads to distant parts of the body. Top Deadly Cancers: Pancreatic, ovarian, lung, glioblastoma, and triple-negative breast cancer are especially difficult to treat and often diagnosed late. Research Focus: Latest advancements focus on personalized, precision medicine tailored to the specific genetic makeup of a patient's tumor and better screening tools for early detection. Prevention: The World Health Organization (WHO) highlights that tobacco use, unhealthy diet, alcohol consumption, and physical inactivity are major risks.
